title: WRING Out The Bias: A Rotation-Based Alternative To Projection Debiasing
claim: Removing a concept by projection can inflate association with unconsidered concepts; rotating within the relevant subspace removes the target bias while preserving the rest.
layout: 2 stacked panels; (a) left-to-right 2D geometry, (b) 3D axes plus bar charts
description: The figure has two panels. Panel (a) is a 2D sketch with orange 'Breed' and teal 'Background' concept axes. An embedding lies almost orthogonal to Breed and is highly associated with Background. A wide arrow labeled 'Removing Background Via Projection' leads to a second sketch. There the embedding sits on the Breed axis, orthogonal to Background and highly associated with Breed. Panel (b) is a 3D sketch with Labrador, Pit Bull, Inside and Outside axes. It shows the original embedding, its projection and its rotation, with a legend for the three marker types. To the right are three columns of small black bar charts: Original, After Projection, and After Rotation (WRING). They show similarity to each concept and the resulting concept bias. Red text says projection 'Increases Breed Bias'. Blue text says rotation 'Maintains Breed Bias'. Orange and teal colors separate the two concept groups.

abstract: Vision-Language models (VLMs), including CLIP, are known to encode biases such as learning spurious correlations that falsely associate background attributes with particular labels. Debiasing approaches typically aim to isolate and remove subspaces corresponding to a target concept via projecting the embedding away from the concept. This strategy succeeds in debiasing VLM embeddings with respect to the concepts considered but can amplify biased shortcuts in unconsidered concepts. In practice, it is impossible to enumerate all possible biases, meaning that an increase in bias can go unobserved during evaluation. We propose a debiasing approach for a set of known concepts such that the relation to the remaining, unconsidered, concepts is minimally changed. We achieve this by rotating the VLM's embeddings within only a relevant subspace, rather than removing these subspaces, which mitigates unintended bias amplification.
